sets.title: Redis protocol, one command per round trip
sets.pin: servers on one core, clients on 20 others
sets.note: Each server on one pinned core, every row at a full core: the rate is one core divided by the cost of an operation. SET and GET draw their keys at random from about a million, as a cache's clients spread them. At depth 1 that cost is mostly the kernel's per-message price, which all three pay alike, so the differences are small and the ranges wide; this VM halts idle vCPUs and every wakeup of a client costs the server a VM exit, which moves a server that answers each command with its own write more than one that batches.

sets.title: Redis protocol, 100 commands per message (pipelined)
sets.pin: servers on one core, clients on 20 others
sets.note: The per-message price divided by a hundred: what remains is parsing and executing commands, where the servers differ. SET and GET draw their keys at random from about a million, more than a core's caches hold, so each lookup waits on memory; SADD, HSET and ZADD put random members into one big collection each.

sets.title: Pipelined, one key
sets.pin: servers on one core, clients on 20 others
sets.note: The same commands on one key, which stays in the core's cache: the easy case for every cache, kept to show parsing and executing alone.

sets.title: Four cores, a cluster-aware client
sets.tool: 5 redis-benchmark processes × 50 connections, 100 commands a message
sets.pin: socketley as four shards and Redis Cluster as four masters, each shard or master pinned to one of the same four cores; five redis-benchmark --cluster processes on 20 others
sets.note: SET and GET draw their keys at random from 1,048,576, 64 behind each of the 16,384 slot tags, preloaded so every GET finds its key (the hit rate is counted every pass). Every shard's mesh counters are read around every timed run: no command crossed between shards in any pass, so the client sent each to its owner. redis-benchmark --cluster's threads spin while they wait, so its client cores are no reading of headroom.

sets.title: Four cores, a plain client at one address
sets.tool: 5 redis-benchmark processes × 50 connections, 100 commands a message
sets.pin: socketley as four shards on one port and Valkey with four I/O threads, on the same four cores; five redis-benchmark processes on 20 others
sets.note: SET and GET draw their keys at random from 1,048,576, three in four of them owned by another shard than the one a connection landed on: socketley carries those over its shard mesh, many commands a frame. LPUSH to ZADD name one key, which one shard owns, so socketley runs those on one of its four cores (see the cores column) and Valkey on its four I/O threads.

sets.title: HTTP: static files and a fixed answer

rows.name: 1 KiB file, a connection per request, 64 at once
fixed answer (Lua handler / nginx return), keep-alive

sets.pin: each server on one core, wrk on 20 others
sets.note: socketley --http dir --http-cache against nginx with one worker, sendfile, open_file_cache and access logs off. Files are .txt: socketley adds a WebSocket script to every .html it serves, by design. The fixed answer is a Lua on_http_request on socketley and a return 200 on nginx, which runs no script at all. Read the 1 KiB keep-alive row with this machine in mind: nginx answers each request with its own write and wakeup, and on this VM waking a halted vCPU costs an exit, which costs a server that does that more than one that batches. A single unpublished pass on another VM (16 cores) read 1.85× for the same row.
sets.caveat: likely higher on this VM than on hardware; see the notes

sets.title: HTTP on four cores

rows.name: 1 KiB file, a connection per request, 64 at once
fixed answer (Lua handler / nginx return), keep-alive

sets.pin: socketley as four shards and nginx with four workers, each pinned to one of the same four cores; wrk (16 threads) on 20 others
sets.note: The same rows as the one-core set, the same wrk for both. socketley spends about twice the CPU a request here that it does on one core, and most of that is the client, not the shards: wrk's threads each hold connections on all four shards, and waking a thread from another core is an interrupt the server's core pays for on loopback, a VM exit on this VM. With one wrk per quarter of the connections, four shards cost about 15% more a request than four separate one-core servers. A client on another machine costs neither.

sets.title: Reverse proxy, HTTP and TCP

rows.name: HTTP, 1 KiB, a connection per request, 64 at once
TCP relay, 1 KiB over HTTP keep-alive, 256 connections

sets.pin: each proxy on one core, the nginx backend on four, wrk on 20
sets.note: All three forward /px/… with the prefix stripped to one nginx backend with four workers, each proxy saturating its core. HAProxy runs one thread with http-reuse always; nginx keeps 256 idle backend connections (keepalive 256); socketley keeps as many backend connections as were busy at once.

sets.title: Reverse proxy on four cores

rows.name: HTTP, 1 KiB, a connection per request, 64 at once
TCP relay, 1 KiB over HTTP keep-alive, 256 connections

sets.pin: socketley as four shards, HAProxy with four threads and nginx with four workers, each pinned to one of the same four cores; the nginx backend (eight workers) on eight others, wrk (16 threads) on 14
sets.note: The same rows as the one-core set, the same wrk for every arm; the backend is not what the proxies run into. As in the server set, each wrk thread holds connections on all four of socketley's shards, so part of every arm's CPU is waking the co-located client across cores.

sets.title: Static site: pages, assets, compression, revalidation

rows.name: page 4 KiB as gzip, the .gz beside it
page 4 KiB as brotli, the .br beside it
page 4 KiB as gzip, no .gz on disk

sets.pin: each server on one core, wrk (8 threads) on 20 others
sets.note: socketley create web --root with its defaults against nginx with one worker, sendfile, open_file_cache, gzip_static and brotli_static, both sending the same headers on plain HTTP (TLS and HTTP/2 are the entrance proxy's). The compressed rows send the same .gz and .br bytes; in the row with no .gz on disk socketley sends a copy it made once and nginx compresses every answer, so that row shows what each does with a site deployed without copies rather than a like-for-like speed. This VM halts idle vCPUs, which costs a server that writes each answer on its own more than one that batches; see the server set.

sets.title: Authoritative DNS, one zone of 10,000 names
sets.tool: dnsperf 8 threads, 32 sockets, 8 s a run, zone of 10000 names
sets.pin: each server one worker on one core, dnsperf on 20 others
sets.note: Queries answered per second of server CPU (rate ÷ cores), because no server saturates its core at a window of 500 outstanding queries, and with more NSD and Knot drop UDP from their default socket buffers and dnsperf waits out each loss. socketley runs with --rrl 0 --proxy none: its response rate limit, on by default, would throttle one client host, and NSD and Knot have none by default. 90% of queries find a name, 10% are NXDOMAIN.

sets.title: MQTT broker, deliveries per second

rows.name: fan-in: 16 publishers to 1 subscriber, QoS 0, 64 B
fan-out: 1 publisher to 100 subscribers, QoS 0, 64 B
fan-out: 1 publisher to 50 subscribers, QoS 1, 64 B
round trip, QoS 1 publish to own delivery

sets.pin: each broker on one core, mqbench on 20 others
sets.note: MQTT 3.1.1, 64-byte payloads; Mosquitto with persistence off and unbounded queues, socketley --anonymous --session-queue 100000. A fan-out delivery costs Mosquitto about 4 µs of CPU, one write each; socketley coalesces the writes to a subscriber, which is the whole of the fan-out difference. The round trip is a QoS 1 publish to the publisher's own subscription.

sets.title: S3 over HTTP, SigV4
sets.tool: warp 1.3.1, 8s a run, SigV4 over plain HTTP

rows.name: PUT 4 KiB, 4 × 16 connections, into an empty store

sets.pin: both servers on the same four cores (socketley as four shards), six warp processes on 20 others
sets.note: MinIO single node, single drive; both on tmpfs, so the comparison is the servers' work and not a disk. MinIO is a Go server that limits itself on one core, hence four for both. At 4 KiB with 64 connections socketley uses under two of its four cores while warp takes fourteen, so that ratio is a floor: the client runs out first. The PUT row starts both servers afresh on empty storage for every pass (five passes), because MinIO reclaims deleted objects in the background and its puts slow while it does.
sets.caveat: a floor: the load generator ran out before socketley did

sets.title: JSON documents over HTTP
sets.tool: loadgen, 8s a run, 100,000 documents, data on tmpfs

rows.name: read one document by id, 64 clients
query on an indexed field, 64 clients

sets.pin: all three on the same four cores (socketley as four shards), loadgen on 20 others
sets.note: 100,000 documents, data on tmpfs. MongoDB through its wire protocol with journaled writes, PocketBase over its REST API with request logs off, socketley over its HTTP API with a key. A sharded socketley db hands every write to shard 0, so its writes are at most what one shard takes, at more cores; reads and queries spread over all four.

sets.title: A TCP service behind an edge

rows.name: round trip through the tunnel, 64 B echo
throughput, 512 MiB echoed through the tunnel

sets.pin: agent and edge (frpc and frps) on the same two cores, the echo service on a third
sets.note: socketley agent and edge against frpc and frps, the service an echo server, one connection. socketley answers a round trip in about half frp's time and moves bulk data at three quarters of its rate.

sets.title: Scraping 100,000 series a second
sets.tool: 50 targets × 2000 series, scraped every 1 s by all three at once

rows.name: range query, 5 min of every path

sets.pin: all three at once on the same two cores, the targets on four others; each pass a 60 s window
sets.note: 50 targets of 2,000 series whose values change every second, scraped every second by all three at the same time, data on tmpfs. socketley's CPU includes its daemon's process. The range query asks five minutes of every path's request rate by status code at a 15 s step, the order of the three rotated.

sets.title: Carrying a directory into a storage
sets.tool: the carriers themselves; the storage target is one socketley storage runtime on other cores

rows.name: first copy, 2000 files of 64 KiB and 50 of 1 MiB

sets.pin: the carrier on two cores, the target storage runtime in a daemon of its own on four others
sets.note: The same socketley storage runtime is the target for both, on tmpfs. rclone is the 1.60 Ubuntu packages (default four transfers); a socketley sync job is one runtime that keeps watching the directory and carries a change when inotify reports it, where rclone walks both sides again. A job's end is read off its figures, which refresh every 250 ms, so each run is made several seconds long.

sets.title: OpenID Connect provider

rows.name: sign-in: authorization code with a password, 16 clients

sets.pin: both on the same four cores (socketley as four shards; Keycloak with its PostgreSQL), idpgen on 20 others
sets.note: 200 accounts. A sign-in is the authorization code flow with PKCE and a password, so it also compares the password hashes each uses by default: scrypt here, PBKDF2 in Keycloak. Keycloak's CPU includes PostgreSQL's. On refresh, userinfo and JWKS socketley uses two and a half of its four cores while idpgen takes up to eleven, so those ratios are floors. Sign-ins come four at a time from each of four addresses: socketley refuses a fifth from one address while four are being checked, and four connections alone may land on two of its four shards, which would measure where the kernel put them. Keycloak's sign-ins still warm up across the passes (145 to 199 a second), so the top of that row's range is its first passes.
sets.caveat: a floor: the load generator ran out before socketley did

sets.title: Mail: delivery in, IMAP and POP3 out
sets.tool: smtp-source (64 processes x 1 connections); mailload.py (8 asyncio processes x 1 connection), 8 s a run

rows.name: SMTP in, 4 KiB messages, 64 connections, 10 a connection
SMTP in, 64 KiB messages, 64 connections, 10 a connection
IMAP: LOGIN, SELECT, FETCH every header of 10,000, 8 clients
IMAP: LOGIN, SELECT, FETCH 1,000 whole 64 KiB messages, 8 clients
POP3: USER, PASS, RETR 1,000 64 KiB messages one by one, 8 clients

sets.pin: every process of each on the same one core (socketley's daemon, idp, storage and mail; Postfix and Dovecot); smtp-source and mailload on 20 others; data on the VM's ext4 disk
sets.note: Postfix hands each message over LMTP to Dovecot's Maildir and index; socketley's mail runtime writes it into its storage runtime. Both sync to disk (about 4 ms a sync here) before a message counts, so the SMTP rows are bound by syncs, not cores, and are timed until the last message is in its mailbox. Every sign-in hashes the password: scrypt in socketley, yescrypt in Dovecot. Dovecot 2.4's lmtp_user_concurrency_limit is set to unlimited, 2.3's default, since 10 made Postfix wait out five-minute retries.

sets.title: MCP server over Streamable HTTP

rows.name: initialize + tools/list, a new session each, 64 at once
tools/call returning 16 KiB of text, 64 sessions

sets.pin: each server on one core, mcpgen on 20 others
sets.note: Against the official MCP SDKs' own servers: the Python SDK under uvicorn with one worker, and the TypeScript SDK on Node as its JSON-response example. All three are driven on revision 2025-11-25 with the initialize handshake, every answer checked. socketley is stateless and issues no session id, so its new session is three requests to the SDKs' four.
